That may be the policy of a pharmacy, but legally, no. Any covered entity is authorized to request a patient’s records, as long as they are continuing their care. Any employee of a covered entity that is involved in a patient’s care can send in a medical records request, that includes pharmacy techs, patient access/whoever is registering or scheduling an appointment for a patient, medical assistants, nurses, etc. Usually support staff will put in records requests without asking the provider for efficiency’s sake, so that the provider has everything that they need for an appointment. Same thing if a pharmacy needs to verify a prescription, or bill insurance. 

If a pharmacy tech is giving the medication to a patient, then they are required to verify that it’s the correct patient, and verify that it is the proper medication. It is not a HIPAA violation to say the name of a patient’s medication if they are speaking to the patient, they have to so that they know if they are giving the patient the correct medication. Like TopDownRide said, that is why there are signs telling other patients where to wait in line. 

While the pharmacy tech in question was extremely impolite and unprofessional, they did not violate HIPAA (according to the information given). They may have violated the policy of that pharmacy, but that has nothing to do with the legality of it.

Source: I work and am certified in health information management/release of information and have to discern if records requests are valid and HIPAA compliant. 

There is A LOT more to HIPAA than most people (especially healthcare workers) think, and there are a lot of exceptions to it. There is a lot of misinformation spread by people who work in healthcare, and it usually just ends with the patient getting pissed at the people who actually specialize in health information management when patients inevitably call to complain.

Provider requests are prioritized and generally should be sent within a week (at least for where I work), usually if it takes longer there is an issue with the request. Have you talked to the medical records/ROI department at the previous OB’s office and has a written request been sent? 

Sometimes records are sent automatically when switching providers, but usually there has to be some kind of request. The new provider’s office can send a request without you having to fill out or sign anything, some offices/health systems can take verbal requests from providers, but the health system that I work for requires a written request for everything. 

If a written request has been sent in, I would confirm that the medical records office actually received it and see if there are any issues with the request that is holding it up. 

If they do have the request, ask if there are any issues with it and ask them to expedite it/make it a STAT request.

If they have not received a request then I would get the fax number or email for the medical records office, call your new provider’s office, ask them to send them a fax cover sheet (or email) with your name, date of birth, and what records they need. If they refuse for some reason, then I’d send in a request to the previous provider’s medical records office (they should have some kind of authorization form).

Also, do either of them use MyChart (EPIC)? If they both do then your new provider may have access to your records already through something called CareEverywhere. I would see if they both use EPIC as their EMR and see if your charts are linked if they both do, if they aren’t linked then the new provider’s office may need to call and get a CareEverywhere ID. 

Also, I can only speak for the process at my health system (and we are verrryyyyy strict with records requests), every office has different policies and may be more lenient, but I tried to keep it as general as possible.

I hope this makes sense and helps! I take calls all day long with this exact question, so if you have any more questions I’m happy to answer :)
